processes: Comparing the same work in different times
plainLanguageExplanation: Power is the speed of doing work — how many joules an engine, muscle, or bulb transfers each second. Its recipe: power = work ÷ time, measured in watts (joules per second). A sprinter and a plodder can both move a 600 J load: the sprinter in one second puts on 600 W; the plodder in three seconds only 200 W. Same work, different rates — that difference is 'power'. The model is a little lift: a box goes up a belt at a speed you choose. Slow turn, the watt meter stays low; flip to fast, the same joules race by and the watts spike. This is why skilled machines, engine displacement, our electric bill's kilowatt-hours and light bulbs all talk in watts — power is the tempo of energy. Turn up the speed, watch the watts run.

whyItMatters: Power is how the world compares engines and athletes: a car's horse-keeping, a sprinter's burst, LED vs. incandescent bulbs, a kettle's boil time. When batteries claim watt-hours and chargers claim watts, they divide by time so you know how fast energy is delivered. Every second sprint, every lightning fast machine, every 'how much can you do in this time' is power made visible.
didYouKnow: A flashlight uses about 1-3 W; a toaster about 1,500 W. If a boy and a machine both do 3,600 J of work but the boy takes 1 min and the machine 6 s, the boy runs at 60 W and the machine at 600 W — ten times the burst in a tenth of the time.
